body.heading: Feelings are like weather
paragraphs: Feelings visit us all day long, the way weather visits the sky. Sometimes it is sunny-happy. Sometimes it rains sad. Sometimes a storm of angry blows through.
Here is the secret: feelings are visitors, not bosses. They can visit. They cannot tell you what to do. And every single one of them passes — even the stormy ones.

body.heading: Meet the visitors
paragraphs: Happy — My heart feels light. I want to smile and share it.
Sad — My heart feels heavy. I might want a hug, a cry, or a quiet minute. Crying is allowed; it is how sadness leaves.
Angry — My body feels hot and tight. My hands want to squeeze. Angry is okay to FEEL. It is not okay to hurt people or things with it.
Scared — My tummy feels fluttery. I want a grown-up close. Scared means my body is trying to protect me.

body.heading: What to do when a big feeling visits
paragraphs: Name it: 'I feel angry.' Naming a feeling makes it smaller, like turning on a light.
Breathe: smell the flower (breathe in), blow the candle (breathe out). Three times.
Tell a grown-up: feelings are always allowed to be told. A good grown-up will listen.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. What feeling is visiting you right now? Point to it on this page.
2. Make the face for each feeling in a mirror. Which face is the funniest? Which is the hardest to make?

takeaway: All feelings are okay to feel — happy, sad, angry, scared. Name it, breathe, tell a grown-up: feelings are visitors, not bosses.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
safetyNotes: Reading only — no physical activity or materials are involved.
screenFreeExtension: Feeling faces game: one person makes a feeling face, the other guesses it and says what might have caused it.
